Kingly Office (of Christ)
KING-lee AW-fiss
n. phrase (Christological / munus triplex)
From Old English cyning (king) + Latin officium (duty, function). In Reformed theology, the kingly office is the third of Christ's mediatorial roles (munus triplex): after His prophetic proclamation and priestly sacrifice, He reigns as the ascended and exalted King over the church, over the nations, and over all creation, with a reign that will be fully manifested at His bodily return.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The kingly office of Christ encompasses His universal authority as the ascended Lord and His present and future reign over all things. Psalm 110:1—the most frequently cited OT text in the NT—provides the foundation: “The LORD said to my Lord, 'Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.'” Psalm 2:6 announces His installation: “Yet I have set My King on My holy hill of Zion.” After the Resurrection, the ascended Christ declares that “all authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth”—an authority that grounds the mission He immediately commissions (Matt 28:18). The Lamb who was slain now reigns: “the Lamb will overcome them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings” (Rev 17:14). Reformed theology distinguishes two aspects of His kingly reign. As King over His church, Christ rules His redeemed people through Word and Spirit, governing His kingdom with laws He alone has the right to prescribe (LBCF 26.2). As King over all things (regnum potentiae), He upholds and governs all creation, providentially directing history toward His appointed end. His kingdom is already present wherever the gospel is believed and obeyed, and will be fully manifested at His bodily return when every knee bows and every tongue confesses (Phil 2:10–11).

Webster 1828 Definition

The mediatorial office by which Christ reigns as King—over His church by Word and Spirit, and over all creation by providential power—an authority declared after His Resurrection and to be fully manifested at His return.

KINGLY OFFICE, n. phrase. The third of Christ's three mediatorial offices (munus triplex). As King, Christ rules with divine authority over His redeemed people and over all creation.

Two aspects: (1) Regnum gratiae (kingdom of grace)—His rule over the church, administered through the Word preached, the sacraments administered, and church discipline exercised; (2) Regnum potentiae (kingdom of power)—His universal providential sovereignty over all nations and all history.

Matt 28:18 is the charter: “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth.” This is not future authority He is yet to receive but present authority He already exercises from the right hand of the Father.

The Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7:12–16) pointed forward to an eternal throne; Christ fulfills it not by sitting on a throne in Jerusalem but by sitting at the right hand of the Majesty on high—the anti-type infinitely greater than the type.

The kingly office grounds both the Great Commission (He sends with authority) and the believer's comfort (He reigns over the circumstances of His people's lives; nothing can befall them outside His sovereign oversight).

Key Scripture

Psalm 110:1 — "The LORD said to my Lord, "Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.""

Psalm 2:6 — ""Yet I have set My King on My holy hill of Zion.""

Matthew 28:18 — "And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, "All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth."

Revelation 17:14 — "These will wage war with the Lamb — and the Lamb will overcome them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings. And those who are with Him are the called and chosen and faithful.""

Modern Corruption

Dispensationalism defers Christ's kingship to a future earthly millennium, making His current session a holding pattern rather than an active reign. Theonomy overextends the kingly office into a mandatory civil program. Both errors mistake the character of Christ's present reign.

expand to see more

Dispensational premillennialism, the 19th-century novelty of John Nelson Darby and later C. I. Scofield, teaches that Christ's Davidic kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected, and consequently postponed—that His current heavenly session is a parenthesis and that His true kingship awaits a future millennial throne in Jerusalem. This directly contradicts the NT witness: Peter at Pentecost proclaims that God has “made this Jesus—whom you crucified—both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36), present tense. Paul declares He must reign “until He has put all His enemies under His feet” (1 Cor 15:25)—a present, ongoing reign. The Reformed confessional tradition uniformly rejects dispensational deferralism.

An opposite error inflates the kingly office into a civil mandate—reconstructionist theonomy, which applies the Mosaic civil code as binding law for Christian nations today. While the Lordship of Christ over all spheres is a biblical truth (the Reformed two-kingdoms tradition rightly affirms it), the specific manner of that lordship in the new covenant era is through the gospel, not Mosaic penology. Christ's kingship governs His church by His Word; it governs nations by common grace and general equity, not by the Sinai civil statutes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Grounded in the Davidic covenant, Psalm 110, and the Resurrection-Ascension, where the risen Christ received all authority and began His universal kingly reign from the Father's right hand.

expand to see more

Hebrew melek — king; the title of the Davidic monarchy that the Messiah would inherit and fulfill (2 Sam 7:12–16; Ps 89).

Greek basileia — kingdom, reign; the rule of Christ as the inaugurated and advancing kingdom of God.

Ps 110:1 — the most-quoted OT verse in the NT, establishing Christ's present exaltation and session at the Father's right hand.

Latin munus — office, gift, duty; the kingly office is one of three mediatorial functions Christ fulfills as the anointed (Christos) Mediator.

Christos — Anointed One; in the OT, anointing set apart prophets, priests, and kings; Jesus is anointed to all three offices at once and supremely.

Usage

"Christ reigns now—the kingly office is not a future program but a present reality exercised through the preaching of the gospel and the governance of His church."

"The Great Commission flows from the kingly office: because all authority belongs to Christ, the church may go to all nations in His name and by His authority."

"Believers find comfort in the kingly office: no enemy, no circumstance, no government, and no demonic power operates outside the sovereign oversight of the King who loves His church."
